t.5.31.1: Placing his joined palms upon his head, the greatly radiant Hanumān, son of the Wind-god, spoke to her, to Sītā, in a sweet voice.
t.5.31.2: Who are you, O blameless one, with eyes like lotus petals and clad in soiled silk, who stand here holding on to the branch of a tree?
t.5.31.3: Why does water born of grief stream from your two eyes, like water scattered from the two petals of a white lotus?
t.5.31.4: Among the Suras and the Asuras, the Nāgas, Gandharvas and Rākṣasas, the Yakṣas and the Kiṃnaras, which one are you, O lovely lady?
t.5.31.5: Who are you, O lovely-faced lady? Are you one of the Rudras, or of the Maruts, or of the Vasus, O fair-hipped one? To me you appear to be a goddess.
t.5.31.6: Is she perhaps Rohiṇī, best among the luminaries, excellent and endowed with every virtue, who, bereft of the Moon, has fallen from the abode of the gods?
t.5.31.7: O auspicious lady, are you not the dark-eyed Arundhatī, who, whether out of anger or out of delusion, has angered your husband Vasiṣṭha?
t.5.31.9: For from the marks and the signs that I observe in you, you seem to me to be the chief queen of a king, a king's daughter.
t.5.31.8: Tell the two of us, O slender-waisted lady: who is it, your son, father, brother, or husband, that has gone from this world to the other world and whom you mourn?
t.5.31.10: If you are Sītā, carried off by force from Janasthāna by Rāvaṇa, then, blessings upon you, tell me this, for I am asking.
t.5.31.11: Having heard his words, Vaidehī, delighted by the praise of Rāma, spoke these words to Hanūmān, who was perched in the tree.
t.5.31.12: I am the daughter of the great-souled Janaka, lord of Videha; Sītā by name am I, the wife of the wise Rāma.
t.5.31.14: Then, in the thirteenth year, the king, together with his preceptors, set about consecrating the delight of the Ikṣvākus with the kingship.
t.5.31.13: For twelve years I dwelt there in the house of Rāghava, enjoying human pleasures, rich in the fulfilment of every desire.
t.5.31.15: But while that consecration of Rāghava was being prepared, the queen named Kaikeyī spoke these words to her husband.
t.5.31.16: I would neither drink nor eat my daily food; if Rāma is consecrated, this will be the end of my life.
t.5.31.17: O best of kings, if that word which you spoke out of affection is not to be made false, then let Rāghava go to the forest.
t.5.31.18: Hearing the cruel and unpleasant words of Kaikeyī, that king, true to his word, remembering the boon he had granted the queen, fell into a swoon.
t.5.31.19: Then the aged king, steadfast in the dharma of truth, weeping, asked his eldest and illustrious son for the kingdom.
t.5.31.20: That glorious one, having first embraced in his mind his father's word, dearer to him even than the consecration, then accepted it with his speech.
t.5.31.21: He would give but never accept; he would not utter anything unkind, not even to save his own life, for Rāma is one whose valor is grounded in truth.
t.5.31.22: That greatly glorious one, casting off his costly upper garments and renouncing the kingdom in his mind, entrusted me to his mother.
t.5.31.23: So I quickly set out ahead of him, to become a forest-dweller, for without him, even a dwelling in heaven holds no delight for me.
t.5.31.24: But even beforehand, the greatly fortunate Saumitri, the delight of his friends, was adorned with garments of tree-bark so that he might follow his elder brother.
t.5.31.26: I am the wife of that hero of boundless might, and while he was dwelling in the Daṇḍaka forest, I was carried off by the evil-souled rākṣasa Rāvaṇa.
t.5.31.25: We, firm in our vows, holding in high regard the command from our master, entered the forest, seen of old, deep and fearsome to behold.
t.5.31.27: Thus a time of two months has been granted to me as a reprieve of life; but beyond those two months, I shall then give up my life.
